FWIW some of the relevant XUL menubar code:

 * https://searchfox.org/firefox-main/source/dom/xul/XULMenuBarElement.cpp
 * https://searchfox.org/firefox-main/source/layout/xul/nsXULPopupManager.cpp
 * https://searchfox.org/firefox-main/source/toolkit/content/widgets/menu.js

Since it was mentioned that you were looking into the activation stuff that's [here](https://searchfox.org/firefox-main/rev/2d38cd5bd7d7958137dd5b4f97aef2f7185a0eb1/dom/xul/XULButtonElement.cpp#350-535).
FWIW the Gecko-only past iteration on menu elements that is removed: https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1372276

Drive-by comment: I noticed that tests are using `:popover-open` for `<menulist>`. I think it would be bad for that pseudo-element to match in this case (same as with `::picker(select)`. The pseudo-class for HTML elements is `:open`. We shouldn't leak the implementation like that.

> Drive-by comment: I noticed that tests are using `:popover-open` for `<menulist>`. I think it would be bad for that pseudo-element to match in this case (same as with `::picker(select)`. The pseudo-class for HTML elements is `:open`. We shouldn't leak the implementation like that.

I don't think it's "leaking" the implementation, if the specification [explicitly says it's a popover](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#select-popover), right? The plan [is similar](https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/12011/changes#diff-41cf6794ba4200b839c53531555f0f3998df4cbb01a4d5cb0b94e3ca5e23947dR65926-R65928) for the menulist element. If the elements are explicitly popovers, it seems odd/confusing for them to only behave partly like a popover, with some popover features magically disabled.

I don't think it's actually defined at the moment? It says "select popover" but other than it being a `div` element it's not explained what that means. I would certainly object to it being defined in a way that would make it match `:popover-open`. But that's https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/issues/10775.

The other algorithms (e.g. [pick an option](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#concept-select-pick)) treat it as a popover, e.g. by running the show popover and hide popover algorithms on it. It sets up an implicit anchor relationship like popovers. Most importantly though, the behavior is observable - if you open the select picker, it participates in the normal popover stacking process, e.g. closing other `popover=auto` popovers on the page. Again, because it **is** a popover.

I'm kind of unclear what the downside of acknowledging it as a popover would be? The upside, for developers, is that they know what it means, how it behaves, and how to use it.

I don’t think we should have multiple APIs for the same thing. An open picker is `select:open`. I also think that participating in numerous popover things should be a case-by-case decision based on what makes sense for the element involved. For instance, we do events separately as well and I don’t think we should allow a button to target a `menulist` as a popover. That’s just rather strange API for a built-in element.
I think it does make sense for select:open to match _and_ for the picker to match :popover-open, but we could limit some of the parsing after picker if we want I guess?
Added Agenda+ to discuss advancing this proposal to Stage 2.  This was previously requested at WHATNOT meeting on December 11, 2025.

I have still some concerns about the current shape (assuming the explainer is up-to-date).
- use of fieldset to group radio|checkbox feels weird.  An attribute in the parent node altogether changes what an element means. And name attribute has worked reasonable well for decades with input elements.
- I can't get my head around pointer event handling when menus and submenus don't seem to nest in DOM. All the *move/*over/*out/*enter/*leave handling becomes, hmm, complicated.
- click handling is still rather unclear but [sounds like](https://github.com/w3c/pointerevents/pull/637#issuecomment-4616264174) there are some possible solutions to that.
The `<fieldset>` discussion in open-ui was in https://github.com/openui/open-ui/issues/1189 , for what it's worth.

Thinking this some more, and it is especially *enter/*leave events which work very well when dealing with nested structures and can be very useful, and they "break" rather badly if subtrees are not nested.

> Thinking this some more, and it is especially *enter/*leave events which work very well when dealing with nested structures and can be very useful, and they "break" rather badly if subtrees are not nested.

If you wouldn't mind - can you give an example of the "useful" use cases that you're thinking about? I'd like to understand better. I'm curious because I'm hoping the use cases aren't about triggering menus, but about something else. Using enter/leave for hover-triggering of submenus is a) handled by the menu elements directly, and b) very tricky to get right. I'd like to make sure that the menu elements take care of the complicated stuff for the developer (in an overridable manner, of course).

*enter/*leave have similar use cases as :hover, hmm, which would also work in a bit surprising way without nested  structure.  Styling the whole open active (pointer over) path would become non-trivial, or some new pseudo classes would be needed.
(`:focus-within` is also broken. Anything hierarchical would not work as expected and require special care.)

> *enter/*leave have similar use cases as :hover, hmm, which would also work in a bit surprising way without nested structure. Styling the whole open active (pointer over) path would become non-trivial, or some new pseudo classes would be needed.

> (`:focus-within` is also broken. Anything hierarchical would not work as expected and require special care.)

I think the behavior of both `:hover`, `focus-within` (plus `:active`) would behave the same either way, actually. Recall that [the spec](https://www.w3.org/TR/selectors-4/#useraction-pseudos) stops these at top layer elements, regardless of DOM structure.

I'm still not sure it's the best thing to just automatically connect user action pseudos and enter/leave events to the entire chain of menus. That might end up getting in the way more than it helps. (Recall that confusion of this sort was the reason for the CSS spec change linked above.) I do think that if there's a use case, we should make it easy to do. But honestly the most common styling pattern is to highlight the ancestor `<menuitem>` when its triggered `<menulist>` is currently open. OpenUI [discussed that use case](https://github.com/openui/open-ui/issues/1363), and came up with the idea to simply have `:open` match the triggering `<menuitem>`. But that has nothing to do with `:hover` or `*enter/*leave`.

Can you help with the use cases you're thinking about where the behavior is surprising or broken?
Well the main reason not to do this is because HTML is an hierarchical format and this is inconsistent with it. And requires ID reference management.
I opened https://github.com/openui/open-ui/issues/1456 for more specific discussion of nested versus non-nested structure for menus.

I [updated](https://github.com/openui/open-ui/pull/1458) the explainer to have [a section on nesting versus idrefs](https://open-ui.org/components/menu.explainer/#should-the-menu-elements-use-id-references-or-nesting-for-submenu-relationships).

A slightly longer update on the question of nesting versus idrefs (cc @annevk @smaug----):

We [discussed](https://github.com/openui/open-ui/issues/1456#issuecomment-4683985964) the issue at the Open UI meeting last week, and I since (as I said above) added a [section](https://open-ui.org/components/menu.explainer/#should-the-menu-elements-use-id-references-or-nesting-for-submenu-relationships) on this topic to the explainer.

As part of adding that section I went through the [existing libraries](https://open-ui.org/components/menu.research/) documented by Open UI library research, and came to a conclusion that disagreed with my previous understanding of the research on existing libraries.  While many libraries express menus as JSON rather than as markup (which I think makes them substantially less relevant to the question, although perhaps not irrelevant) and a bunch of the libraries don't appear to document a way to do submenus, I found three libraries that both described menus with markup and supported submenus.  All three used a nested structure.  Two of the three ([Material Web](https://github.com/material-components/material-web/blob/main/docs/components/menu.md) and [React Spectrum](https://react-spectrum.adobe.com/v3/Menu.html)) avoided nested interactives ("Option B") while the third ([Semantic UI](https://semantic-ui.com/collections/menu.html)) took the approach with nested interactive elements ("Option C").

Given the various discussions (in WHATNOT and OpenUI) and that additional research my current plan is to start work on updating the proposal (prototype, explainer, and HTML spec PR) to an approach that uses nesting, along the lines of Option B in https://github.com/openui/open-ui/issues/1456, meaning something like:
```html
<menubar>
  <submenu>
    <menulabel>File</menulabel>
    <menulist>
      <menuitem>New</menuitem>
      <menuitem>Open</menuitem>
    </menulist>
  </submenu>
  <submenu>
    <menulabel>Edit</menulabel>
    <menulist>
      <menuitem>Cut</menuitem>
      <menuitem>Copy</menuitem>
      <menuitem>Paste</menuitem>
    </menulist>
  </submenu>
</menubar>
```

This update would mean dropping the commands-related parts of the proposal, but continuing to make menulists be popovers.

I'm interested in feedback on this plan -- and preferably sooner than later -- since what this plan likely means is that I'm going to spend the next few weeks revising the prototype, explainer, and spec, and then try to resume the discussion about moving this proposal to Stage 2.

Two clarifications, it's unclear to me how this works for the button opening a menu case which we did want to support?

Also by removing commands do you mean just the toggle-menu command or do you mean removing command/commandfor from menuitems too? Because they're a useful feature regardless.

> Two clarifications, it's unclear to me how this works for the button opening a menu case which we did want to support?

I think the simplest answer for that case is that either (a) you can style a menubar to look like a button or (b) you can put a vertically-oriented menubar inside a (non-menu) popover that is opened by the button.  Alternatively, we could add something back, but we'd need to figure out what the right markup structure is for it.

> Also by removing commands do you mean just the toggle-menu command or do you mean removing command/commandfor from menuitems too? Because they're a useful feature regardless.

Oops.  Indeed, `command` and `commandfor` would continue to be on `menuitem`; we'd just be dropping the `toggle-menu` command so that we'd no longer have any commands that open/close menus.

Based on prototyping since the June 17 meeting I think I expect to be able to bring this back for re-discussion next week, so I've readded `agenda+`.  (I still need to make some explainer updates prior to that discussion that I haven't made yet, though.)

Also, a further reply to @lukewarlow's https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11729#issuecomment-4724143447 -- while prototyping the changes and updating tests, I came to the conclusion that a reasonable path forward for the button-opens-a-menulist use case is the following (which essentially means changing slightly less than I was previously planning to change):
* loose `<menulist>` elements not in a `<submenu>` are still allowed as they were before, and still are implicit popovers
* a `<button>` can invoke them with the `show-popover`/`hide-popover`/`toggle-popover` commands, or with the `popovertarget` attribute.  (But the `toggle-menu` command still goes away.)
* `<button>` elements doing the above are still implicitly `aria-haspopup=menu`

Oh, and as to the question of how to do radio and checkbox menuitems that was discussed in https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11729#issuecomment-4621448600 -- there's a bit of discussion in https://github.com/openui/open-ui/issues/1189, but I think a key question for how to move forward is whether there are strong preferences between option 1, option 3, or option 4 (see [options 1 & 2](https://github.com/openui/open-ui/issues/1189#issue-2985964493) and [options 3 & 4](https://github.com/openui/open-ui/issues/1189#issuecomment-4663159156)).

So far I think @lukewarlow expressed a preference for option 1 (distinct `<menuitemcheckbox>` and `<menuitemradio>` elements), whereas I think I prefer option 3 (which intentionally imitates the way `<input>` becomes a checkbox or a radio).

(I think @annevk and @smaug---- may have opinions.)
Fwiw my actual preference is still for option 2, but failing that I lean towards option 1.
I'm curious what the concrete concern with `fieldset` or a grouping element of that nature is. As far as I can tell there's no use for names here so they end up being redundant.
The concern is (in)consistency with other features in the platform. And that parent element would altogether change the meaning of the child elements..

Yes, but there's no natural way to make them consistent here I think, is there? Perhaps we can do some combination of options, whereby we introduce a new element for a checkable (`menucheckable`?) and use a parent element to indicate grouping and exclusivity.

> And that parent element would altogether change the meaning of the child elements..

This is already the case in a number of places, especially for acc-tree calculations. Even behavioural differences, I can think of at least `<summary>` and `<option>` that behave different when outside their container than when inside. Even in some ways a button element behaves differently when it's inside a form than when it's outside a form.

A `<menuitemcheckable>` + some container element doesn't seem too bad if we did want to have a different element to take on the menuitemradio/menuitemcheckbox role.

I think it's worth noting that one of the strong pieces of feedback in favor of a grouping element (e.g., in https://github.com/openui/open-ui/issues/1189#issuecomment-4814143764) is that it's bad authoring practice to do anything other than have a consecutive run of checkable or radio menuitems.  In particular, a group of radio or checkbox menu items should not be separated by other menuitems or anything else.  So having a parent element that controls radio/checkbox state helps push authors toward following good practices.

Another rationale is that there was a desire for a rendered caption/legend for a group of radio or checkbox menuitems, and `<fieldset>` + `<legend>` provide this somewhat naturally.  (Note that I haven't yet worked on or investigated rendering aspects of this in Chromium's current prototype implementation, and I was holding off until the discussion of whether we'd actually use `<fieldset>` was sorted out... so odds are it doesn't yet look reasonable.)
Not even `<hr>`? I certainly see that being used to break up long lists of checkable items that are all mutually exclusive in platform menus.
Yeah, `<hr>` seems reasonable (to me at least); I think the main concern is mixing with other `<menuitem>`s.

fwiw, i like the idea of `menuitemcheckable` or whatever that ends up getting named, as there can be legit reasons to have a single checkbable menuitem in a menulist, and it would be far easier to just be able to declare that one element, rather than having to setup a fieldset with an attribute to identify it as checkable to contain a single menuitem.

but, a menuitemradios really need to be grouped, and shouldn't have other non-radios intermixed with them since that can make it unclear which items will impact the state of another when checked.

re: the `hr` element - as of now `hr` on the web does very little to indicate a separation / grouping of menuitems or options in the accessibility tree.  it's more of a visual separator, which isn't very helpful in programmatically identifying a clear start/end point to a group of menuitems or options like a named fieldset or optgroup would be.  and as david said, `hr` separators wouldn't do much in helping prevent authors from intermixing menuitems/radios/checkboxes together, since there's no real "group" that is created to help enforce that.

From https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11729#issuecomment-4811885367 I'd still prefer option 3.  I'm trying to understand what the issues with that are.
Are the problems in different approaches listed somewhere?

re @smaug---- 's:
> From [#11729 (comment)](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11729#issuecomment-4811885367) I'd still prefer option 3. I'm trying to understand what the issues with that are. Are the problems in different approaches listed somewhere?

I've expanded the [section of the explainer](https://open-ui.org/components/menu.explainer/#how-best-to-represent-checkable-menuitems) that discusses this in an attempt to answer this question better.  There's also even slightly more detail in https://github.com/openui/open-ui/issues/1189#issuecomment-4928386129 and earlier comments in that issue.
Moving to stage 2 per today's WHATNOT meeting discussion.

I think the PR in #12011 is at the point where some review of the PR itself would be useful.  It's probably not quite ready for a full line-by-line review, but I think it would be useful to review for the following questions:
* Does it contain the right pieces?  In other words, are there things missing from the PR that should be part of it, or things in it that shouldn't be?  (I think this is also the question that's required for advancement to Stage 3.)  That said, I certainly expect to find some missing things in the future, but I don't know of one right now other than the ones covered by TODO comments in the PR.
* Is there any feedback on the TODO comments in the PR that ask questions about the correct approach to take?
Moved to stage3 per the discussion in today's WHATNOT meeting.

Why is the PR's OP not up-to-date? It also doesn't seem like the PR defines the `orientation` attribute?

I'm also rather surprised this contains a whole section on the controversial interest invokers feature (including re-introducing the "invoker" word which we've largely managed to get rid of in the specification).

> Why is the PR's OP not up-to-date? It also doesn't seem like the PR defines the `orientation` attribute?

Oops.  I think I've updated it now, although it's possible that a little more detail might be desirable.  (Sorry for missing this -- I was making an effort to keep the explainer, spec PR, and Chromium implementation in sync with each other, and managed to forget about keeping the PR's OP up-to-date too!)

I've also clarified the OP that the point it was making about `orientation` is that it's *not* included in the current PR, though I added a little explanation as to why that's still the case, and that we now intend not to include it as part of the initial version of menus.

> I'm also rather surprised this contains a whole section on the controversial interest invokers feature (including re-introducing the "invoker" word which we've largely managed to get rid of in the specification).

My understanding of the core controversy around interest invokers is that it centers on the risks of authors creating content that can *only* be opened or activated via interest and not by a broader set of mechanisms that (combined) meet accessibility requirements better.  The menu elements proposed here use the mechanisms of the interest invokers proposal for opening submenus in response to hover (in a way that roughly matches the way menus work across major desktop operating systems), but they do so in a way that avoids this core controversy because submenus also open on click/tap or on keyboard activation.  (In other words, my understanding of the core of the controversy is that it's specific to the risks of exposing the mechanism to authors and does not apply to using it internally in other specification features, as long as those specification features themselves follow the correct practices.)

I think it's valuable to use the internals of the specification proposal for interest invokers for a few reasons:
* if we do find a way forward to make progress on the developer-exposed interest invokers API surface, we probably want menus to interact well with it, and building on top of it should do that
* even if we don't, it's possible (although this point is definitely less concrete than the other two) we might add *other* features to HTML that also want to build on it in the same way, and *those* should interact well with menus
* the internals of the interest invokers spec proposal are based on quite a bit of prototyping and testing, and I think if we tried to write a new (simpler?) proposal for just the parts that we think menus need, we might end up finding and re-fixing many of the same bugs that have already been fixed as part of the prototyping cycles that have gone in to the interest invokers work, and we may well end up back at a similar level of complexity.

That said, I'm totally open to changing the names.  I wasn't aware that "invoker" was a word we wanted to avoid and I'm happy to rename things as needed.
